newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco company asks for new trial in Florida case.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco company asks for new trial in Florida case.

text.p: A Florida judge was set to hear arguments Tuesday from lawyers for Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. who are seeking to overturn a jury award of $750,000 to a smoker with lung cancer.

In a motion filed with the court, Brown & Williamson claimed the Aug. 9 verdict was "erroneous and contrary to the law" and cites more than 100 reasons why it should be overturned or a new trial should be granted.

A six-member circuit court jury ruled that Brown & Williamson was negligent and made a dangerous and defective product in the case of Grady Carter of Orange Park, Florida, who smoked for 50 years until he was diagnosed with lung cancer in 1991.
The judgment was just the second rendered against the tobacco industry and sent shock waves through the market, causing tobacco stocks to plunge.
The only other time the industry had lost a product liability case was in 1988, when a jury awarded $400,000 to the family of Rose Cipollone. The judgment was overturned on appeal.

In the Florida case, the jury awarded $500,000 to Carter and $250,000 to his wife Millie. Carter smoked Lucky Strikes, made by American Tobacco Co., from 1947 to 1972, when he began smoking other brands.
Brown & Williamson, in its petition, asked for a direct verdict, a judgment notwithstanding the jury verdict, or a new trial.

The company, a successor by merger to American Tobacco, alleged trial Judge Brian Davis erred in admitting testimony about the adequacy of federal warning labels, and said the plaintiff's theory that its products were defective should have been rejected by the court.
It was uncertain whether Davis would rule Tuesday after hearing arguments from the company and Carter's lawyers.
Brown & Williamson is a unit of Britain's B.A.T Industries PLC.
